method: Moving the sight pin by d rotates the line of sight relative to the arrow by d divided by the sight radius, so at a target distance D the point of impact moves by D x d / sight radius. Inverted, the correction is d = sight radius x error / D with the error and the distance in the same unit: a 762 mm sight radius and a group 50 mm (5 cm) high at 30 m needs 762 x 50 / 30000 = 1.27 mm of sight movement, and the same sight at 60 m needs 0.64 mm for the same error. The direction follows the rule of chasing the arrow: the sight moves toward the group, so a high group calls for raising the sight, which then makes the arrow land lower, and a group to the right calls for moving the sight right. A click value set on the sight converts the movement into clicks, so a sight that moves 0.1 mm per click needs about 12.7 clicks for that example. Imperial inputs take the sight radius and group error in inches and the distance in yards, converting at 36 inches per yard. Accepted ranges are a sight radius of 50 to 1500 mm (2 to 60 in), a distance of 3 to 100 m (3 to 110 yd), group errors within +/- 200 cm (+/- 80 in) and a click value of 0.01 to 5 mm (0.001 to 0.2 in); the page warns when a correction would exceed 4 mm. This is geometric guidance only: it assumes a straight line of sight to the pin and it ignores arrow speed, trajectory shape and form errors, so confirm any large change with a test group. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Sight correction geometry: a pin moved by d rotates the line of sight by d / sight radius, shifting the point of impact by distance x d / sight radius
Direction rule: move the sight toward the group (chase the arrow), so raising the sight for a high group lowers the point of impact
Typical recurve sight radius is 600 to 900 mm between the peep or eye and the sight pin, and shorter on many compound setups
